analysis.investment_thesis: Aaradhya fails the Magic Formula decisively — a 0.45% ROE implies near-zero return on capital, meaning this is not a "good business" at any price. The 12.4x P/E (~8% earnings yield) is mediocre and not cheap enough to compensate for the capital inefficiency in a commodity paper business.
key_strengths: Positive earnings (P/E 12.4x) — EBIT likely positive, so formula is computable
Small 159 Cr market cap leaves theoretical room for operational improvement
key_risks: ROE of 0.45% indicates abysmal return on capital — Magic Formula's #1 disqualifier
Commodity paper industry with no pricing power or moat
Tiny microcap in a capital-intensive business — low FCF conversion likely
red_flags: ROE 0.45% is essentially zero — capital is being destroyed or barely preserved
If ROE is 0.45% and P/E is 12.4x, net margin must be razor-thin — earnings quality suspect
Paper products = commodity with high capex intensity, structurally low ROIC
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks stocks on two axes: how cheap (earnings yield) and how good (return on capital). Aaradhya ranks catastrophically on the "good business" axis — a 0.45% ROE is roughly 1/50th of what I consider investable (~20%+ ROIC). Even if EBIT/Capital is somewhat higher than ROE due to leverage mechanics, this level of return indicates the business cannot compound capital. In Greenblatt's framework, a cheap bad business is still a bad business — you do not want to own companies earning sub-FD returns on shareholder equity, regardless of valuation.

The 12.4x P/E translates to roughly an 8% earnings yield, which is below my 12%+ threshold for "attractive" and nowhere near the 15%+ needed to compensate for a structurally weak business. Paper & paper products is a commodity industry with heavy capex and cyclical pricing — exactly the kind of capital-intensive sector where Magic Formula economics rarely work. Promoter holding of 70.58% is the only mild positive, but alignment cannot rescue sub-1% ROE. This is a clear AVOID; there are thousands of Indian listed names with better earnings-yield and ROIC combinations.
